options: The shell, before the program starts
The program, using a library function
The kernel, during execve
The filesystem, when the path is opened
drills.why: Which is why every program agrees about globbing without any of them implementing it, and why a program wanting the pattern makes you quote it.

drills.q: What does the argument vector contain for a pattern matching three files?
options: Three arguments, one per file
One argument, the pattern
Four arguments, the pattern and the files
One argument, the files joined by spaces
drills.why: Measured with a program that prints its own arguments. By the time it runs there is no pattern anywhere.

drills.q: Why does a directory with very many files produce an argument list too long?
options: The limit is on the vector the shell is building
The program cannot allocate that many strings
The filesystem cannot list that many names
The kernel refuses to open that many files
drills.why: The program never gets far enough to have an opinion, because the failure is in handing the vector over.

drills.q: A pattern matches nothing. What happens?
options: It depends on the shell: one passes the literal through, another refuses to run
Every shell passes the literal through
Every shell refuses to run
The command runs with no argument in its place
drills.why: Measured: bash passes *.nope through as an argument and zsh reports no matches found. Both are defensible policy decided in the gap.

options: After variable substitution, on the result
Before substitution, on the literal text
Inside the program, on its arguments
Only for values containing a glob character
drills.why: Which is exactly why a filename with a space breaks a script written without quotes.

drills.q: What does quoting a variable reference do?
options: Skips the splitting step, so the value arrives as one argument
Prevents the substitution
Escapes any special characters in the value
Nothing, unless the value contains a glob
drills.why: A value of three words gives three arguments unquoted and one quoted, which the argument printer confirms directly.

drills.q: Where does a redirection appear in the argument vector?
options: Nowhere
As two arguments, the operator and the target
As one argument, the whole phrase
As an extra entry after the last argument
drills.why: It is an instruction to the shell, and instructions to the shell do not survive into the vector.

drills.q: A command that does not exist is redirected into a file. What happens to the file?
options: It is created and left empty, because the open happened first
Nothing; the command failed before anything opened
It keeps its old contents
It is created only if the shell reports no error
drills.why: That ordering is why a failing command still truncates its output file, and why reading and writing the same file in one command destroys it.

drills.q: In the gap between fork and exec, what is the child?
options: Still the shell, running shell code
Already the requested program
A stub the kernel provides
An empty process with no code
drills.why: It opens the redirections, moves descriptors, sets its process group and restores signal handling, and only then calls execve.

drills.q: Why does redirection need no cooperation from the program?
options: The program writes to descriptor 1 and somebody else decided what it refers to
Programs are compiled with redirection support
The kernel intercepts writes and reroutes them
The shell rewrites the program's output afterwards
drills.why: Which is the whole reason the mechanism composes with every program ever written, including ones older than the shell you are using.

drills.q: How many processes does a three-stage pipeline create?
options: Three, running at once
One, running the stages in turn
Two, since the shell runs the last stage itself
Four, one per stage and one to coordinate
drills.why: Counted directly while it ran. The second stage consumes while the first is still producing, which is why a slow filter still shows output early.

drills.q: What is the exit status of a pipeline?
options: The last stage's
The first failure's
The largest of the stages'
Zero if any stage succeeded
drills.why: Measured: false into true gives 0 and exit 7 into exit 9 gives 9, so a script can report success after the important half failed.

drills.q: Why can cd not be a separate program?
options: The working directory is per-process state and there is no call to change another process's
It would be too slow to fork for it
The shell needs to update its prompt
Programs are not permitted to change directory
drills.why: A child shell that changes directory reports the new one while the parent still reports the old one.

drills.q: Why can a script not change your shell's directory?
options: Running it forks, and sourcing it does not
Scripts are denied that permission
The change is undone when the script exits
Only builtins may appear in scripts
drills.why: Same mechanism as the previous one, seen from the other side.

drills.q: Which of these does a program see after execve?
options: An exported variable and an inherited open descriptor
Every shell variable and every open descriptor
Only the arguments
Exported variables only, since descriptors are closed
drills.why: An unexported variable was never put in the copy handed over. A descriptor survives unless it was marked close-on-exec, which is the mechanism every redirection depends on and a real bug class besides.
